They urged Him: "Stay with us." The invitation—offered to a stranger, not yet knowing His name—opened the door. Our hospitality to the unknown guest is sometimes an invitation to know Him.
At the table, He took bread, blessed it, and broke it—the gestures they would recognize. What they had seen Him do in that upper room, they would see again. The pattern of His love does not change.
Their eyes opened, and they knew Him—then He vanished. Recognition and absence came together. The point was not to see Him stay, but to know that He lives.

"Weren't our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us?" Only then did they understand what they had felt. The Holy Spirit was awakening them while His words opened the Scripture. Truth recognizes itself.
They rose up that very hour and ran back to Jerusalem—the same road they had walked away from, now urgent with hope. When you know the Lord is alive, you run toward His people.

"The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!" Before the Emmaus disciples could speak, they heard that He had appeared to Peter. The Risen One appeared to many; His presence broke through from every side.
They told how He was recognized in the breaking of the bread—a sign that would echo through the centuries. His work with His hands, His sharing, His sacrifice—these remain how we know Him.
Jesus stood among them and said, "Peace be to you." Not "Peace I leave you" but "Peace be to you"—the living greeting of the Risen Christ to His frightened community.
They were terrified, thinking they had seen a spirit. Joy and terror mixed—the knowledge that something real and beyond the ordinary had entered the room.
"Why are you troubled? Why do doubts arise in your hearts?" He does not rebuke them harshly but gently asks them why they are held back—as if to say, I am here, why not hope?
"Touch me and see—a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones as I have." He is not a phantom or a memory. Resurrection is bodily, real, verifiable. The Lord has substance; He is not an idea.
He showed them His hands and feet. The marks of crucifixion remained on the Risen Lord—the scars that proved His identity, evidence that redemption cost Him everything.
They still didn't believe for joy—overcome by feeling too large for belief to hold. Sometimes happiness is so unexpected that we cannot quite grasp it as real.
They offered Him broiled fish and honeycomb. The tenderness of the gesture—feeding Him, as if to welcome Him back to the table, to living. Resurrection and ordinary meal become one.
He ate in front of them. The Risen Lord takes food, sits with His people—not as a specter, but as one who inhabits a redeemed body that can taste and share.

"All things written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me must be fulfilled." Every Scripture finds its center in Him. He does not contradict the Old Covenant; He completes it.

He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. Not just their eyes or ears, but their minds—the seat of understanding. The Spirit must illuminate; knowledge of God requires an opening from above.

"Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day." Here is the pattern: suffering, death, resurrection. Not as accident, but as necessity written in God's plan.

"Repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem." From the place of rejection comes the proclamation of forgiveness. Mercy flows backward into the place of shame.
"You are witnesses of these things." The disciples are called to testify. Not to write, not to philosophize, but to witness—to tell what they have seen and touched and come to know.

"Wait in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high." They are not sent immediately but told to wait. The gift of the Spirit will come; they are to prepare their hearts in expectation.
He led them out as far as Bethany—the place where He had raised Lazarus, a place already marked by resurrection power. There He lifted up His hands and blessed them, a priestly gesture of completion.
While He blessed them, He withdrew and was carried up into heaven. The blessing continues even as He ascends. His physical presence departs; His benediction remains.
They worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy. Departure did not bring sorrow but worship and joy—the paradox of Easter faith, where loss and triumph meet.

They were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God—and readers today hear an echo in that joy. The disciples knew a secret that the empty tomb whispers still: death has been answered. Our worship joins theirs across the centuries.
